To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following factors discriminate between lower socioeconomic status, largely Mexican-American, patients who continue in treatment at our clinic for a few visits and those who continue for many visits: self referral, age, marital status, and complaints of social or family incompatability, anxiety or depression.

(1) Mexican-Americans are more likely than Anglos to be referred for treatment by a third party; (2) Mexican-Americans are less likely to be self-referrals; (3) Mexican-Americans who are self-referrals tend to be younger; (4) Mexican-Americans tend to be more depressed; (5) Mexican-Americans tend not to be married or are more likely to be separated or divorced; and (6) Mexican-Americans tend more frequently to have financial and situational problems.

the Mexican-American clients of the Barrio Mental Health Service who were self-referred, older, and who complained of anxiety, depression or social or family incompatability tended to continue in treatment for a longer period of time than clients who were not self-referred, younger, and who complained only of financial or situation problems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
factors associated with length of treatment in a mental health service.
the identification of those factors which differentiate the short from the long treatment patient in a mental health service for Mexican-Americans.
the development of a community mental health programme in a barrio-neighbourhood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the short treatment contact patient is a Mexican-American, young, single male, who is self-referred and has complaints of anxiety, social or family conflict.
a number of variables were found to be associated with length of treatment in this barrio-neighborhood mental health service.

the factors associated with short treatment are : (a) the patient's own referral, (b) the patient's age, (c) the patient's marital instability, (d) the patient's complaint of anxiety, depression or social or family in-compatibility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the short contact Mexican-American patient is more likely to be self-referred, younger, married, and have a complaint of depression or anxiety, and that the long contact patient is more likely not to be self-refered, older, unmarried, and have a financial or situation complaint.
the long treatment patient is a young, single, self-referred, Mexican-American with complaints of anxiety, and social incompatibility.

the long treatment patient is a young, married, self-referred, non-Anglo, with complaints of anxiety, social and family incompatibilities and marital instability, and that he continues in treatment longer than the short treatment patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the factors which predict long treatment contact are not the same as those which predict long treatment in a clinic serving middle class Anglo patients.

the factors which differentiate short from long term treatment contact are not those which have been found to be important in other studies, and that the short term patient is not the one who is more disturbed, but rather one who has less motivation for treatment and less social support.
the factors that are associated with long term treatment are different for different groups of people.
